title: "Bootstrap confidence intervals"

The sampling distribution of a median is less convenient than that of a mean. The [**nonparametric bootstrap**](https://openintro-ims.netlify.app/foundations-bootstrapping.html) approximates it by repeatedly sampling observed units with replacement and recalculating the statistic.

The bootstrap substitutes the empirical distribution $\widehat F_n$, which places mass $1/n$ on each observed unit, for an unknown population distribution $F$. Sampling from $\widehat F_n$ requires replacement; without replacement, every size-$n$ resample would contain exactly the observed rows and the statistic would never vary. This is the same empirical-sampling logic introduced for [estimators](properties-of-estimators.qmd#estimators-are-random-variables).

The resulting endpoints are interpreted through the repeated-sampling definition of a [confidence interval](confidence-intervals.qmd). The spread of the bootstrap statistics estimates the estimator's [standard error](standard-errors.qmd), while their standard deviation retains the meaning introduced on the [standard-deviation page](../random-variables-and-distributions/standard-deviation.qmd).

We begin by stating the resampling algorithm, apply it to the adult-women median, and then separate what the resulting interval estimates from what its empirical bootstrap approximation cannot guarantee.

## The algorithm

For observed speaker values $x_1,\ldots,x_n$:

1. Draw $n$ speaker rows with replacement from the empirical distribution.
2. Calculate the bootstrap statistic $T_b^*$.
3. Repeat for $b=1,\ldots,B$.
4. Use the empirical quantiles $Q^*_{\alpha/2}$ and $Q^*_{1-\alpha/2}$ as percentile endpoints.

Thus the percentile interval is

$$
[Q^*_{\alpha/2},Q^*_{1-\alpha/2}].
$$

Keep four objects separate: $T(\mathbf X)$ is the estimator under the population model, $T(\mathbf x)$ is the observed statistic, $T_b^*$ is the statistic in bootstrap sample $b$, and the empirical distribution of the $T_b^*$ values is the bootstrap distribution. The percentile method uses the last object's quantiles as endpoints because it treats its displacement and shape as an approximation to those of the sampling distribution.

This approximation tends to work best for smooth statistics with modest bias and a sampling distribution that the empirical distribution can reproduce. Medians from small or highly discrete samples can yield repeated bootstrap values; strong bias or skewness can make percentile endpoints inaccurate. Exact inversion would require a specified finite-sample reference distribution whose tail probabilities can be solved for the parameter. The percentile procedure instead substitutes empirical resampling quantiles, so its coverage is approximate.

## Bootstrapping the adult-women median

The target statistic is the median duration of /I/ in *hid* among the observed Hillenbrand adult women. Since this subset has one row per speaker, resampling its rows is speaker-block resampling.

```{r}
#| label: bootstrap-hillenbrand-median
library(ggplot2)

vowels <- read.csv(
  "data/hillenbrand/vowels-complete.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
women_hid <- subset(vowels, speaker_type == "woman" & vowel == "I")
x <- women_hid$duration_ms
observed_median <- median(x)

set.seed(20261021)
B <- 10000L
bootstrap_medians <- replicate(
  B,
  median(sample(x, size = length(x), replace = TRUE))
)
bootstrap_interval <- unname(quantile(bootstrap_medians, c(0.025, 0.975), type = 7))
bootstrap_se <- sd(bootstrap_medians)

data.frame(
  speakers = length(x),
  observed_median_ms = observed_median,
  bootstrap_replicates = B,
  bootstrap_se_ms = bootstrap_se,
  lower_ms = bootstrap_interval[1],
  upper_ms = bootstrap_interval[2]
)
```

The bootstrap standard error is `r sprintf("%.3f", bootstrap_se)` ms, and the percentile interval is [`r sprintf("%.3f", bootstrap_interval[1])`, `r sprintf("%.3f", bootstrap_interval[2])`] ms.

```{r}
#| label: plot-bootstrap-hillenbrand-median
#| fig-cap: "Bootstrap distribution of the adult-women /I/ median. The line marks the observed median."
ggplot(data.frame(median_ms = bootstrap_medians), aes(median_ms)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), binwidth = 1,
                 fill = "grey75", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = observed_median, color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Bootstrap median /I/ duration (ms)", y = "Bootstrap density") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

If all twelve vowel rows had been retained, the bootstrap would need to resample speakers as blocks so that their vowel measurements remained together. Under the [definition of independence](../foundations/independence.qmd), row-wise resampling would impose independent vowel-token draws that the repeated-speaker design does not supply. The interval is also conditional on treating the observed cohort as an empirical approximation to the target distribution.

The code mirrors the algorithm: `sample(x, ..., replace = TRUE)` draws one empirical-distribution sample, `median()` computes $T_b^*$, `replicate(B, ...)` constructs the bootstrap distribution, and `quantile(..., c(0.025, 0.975))` selects the percentile endpoints.

## Recap and forward link

1. Replacement is what makes repeated size-$n$ samples from the empirical distribution vary.
2. The bootstrap distribution approximates the sampling distribution; it is not identical to it.
3. The percentile interval inherits limitations from bias, skewness, discreteness, dependence, and the observed cohort.

The [null-hypothesis page](null-hypotheses-and-test-statistics.qmd#the-null-and-statistic) returns to the paired vowel difference and formalizes a null comparison.

## Check your understanding

1. Why does the bootstrap sample with replacement?
2. What makes the resampling unit a speaker here?
3. What does `bootstrap_se` estimate?
4. Which population limitation does the bootstrap leave unchanged?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Sampling with replacement draws from the empirical distribution and allows observed speakers to appear zero, one, or several times across bootstrap samples. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The analyzed subset contains one /I/ duration per adult-woman speaker, so one row is one speaker. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. `bootstrap_se` estimates the standard deviation of the bootstrap sampling distribution of the sample median. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The bootstrap interval remains conditional on the observed Hillenbrand cohort and does not supply population-representative recruitment. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
